content: The term deaf-mute was historically used by hearing individuals to describe a person who was both deaf and unable to speak. In earlier times, this term was socially acceptable and often used to refer to deaf individuals who communicated using sign language. However, it is now considered offensive, much like how the term colored was once used to describe African Americans but is now regarded as derogatory. The preferred term today is simply deaf. The phrase deaf-mute first appeared in the Code of Hammurabi, an ancient set of laws from the Near East dating back to 1700 BC. It is also mentioned in ancient Greek writings from the 7th century BC. While the term is still occasionally used in historical contexts to describe deaf individuals who cannot speak or choose not to speak due to the negative attention their atypical voices might attract, it is now largely viewed as outdated and inappropriate. Additionally, the term has sometimes been used in jest or as a metaphor to describe hearing individuals who refuse to use common sense or are unreliable. Other historical terms used to describe deaf individuals include deaf and dumb, semi-deaf, and semi-mute. Of these, only deaf and dumb persists in some references, though it carries connotations of insensitivity and is generally considered insulting, inaccurate, and socially or politically incorrect. From antiquity, as noted in the Code of Hammurabi, to more recent and less enlightened times, terms like deaf-mute and deaf and dumb were even equated with idiot by some hearing individuals. In Europe and Western societies, most deaf individuals are taught to speak, with varying levels of success in terms of ability and fluency. Since the establishment of public deaf education in the 18th century, the simple identity of deaf has been embraced by the signing deaf community and remains the preferred term of reference or identity. In literature and art, the term deaf-mute has been used in various contexts. In J.D. Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye, the phrase is used to describe someone who does not express their thoughts and hears nothing, effectively isolating themselves from the world. In Ken Kesey’s One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest, the character Chief Bromden is believed by others to be a deaf-mute, though he can actually hear and speak. He conceals this because, during his upbringing, he was ignored and not spoken to, metaphorically making him deaf and mute. In the film Babel, the character Chieko Wataya, a deaf teenage girl played by Rinko Kikuchi, is referred to several times in the English subtitles as a deaf-mute, though the accuracy of the subtitles in translating the Japanese reference to her deafness is unclear. Similarly, in Carson McCullers’ 1940 novel The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter, the character Singer is repeatedly referred to as a deaf-mute.
